Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Review the historical context and precedence on the reason sex- and gender-specific analysis
are important.
Define sex and gender and distinguish between sex- and gender-related variables in a
research context.
Identify methods for integrating sex and gender in all phases of research, from literature
review to knowledge translation.
Historical Perspective
Evolution of Sex-Specific Analysis

Before the 1990s, biomedical research mainly focused on the male model, with the
assumption that male biology was representative of both sexes in fields not related to the
reproductive system. In 1985, the US Public Health Service assembled the Task Force on
Women’s Health Issues, which authored a 34-page report outlining the lack of knowledge of
female biology and explaining how advances in research, practice, policy, education, and
public programs would improve the health of women, especially minority and underprivileged
women.1
After the task force report, the National Institutes of Health (NIH) issued a policy in 1986 for
the inclusion of women in clinical research. In 1993, the NIH Revitalization Act was passed by
Congress, turning this policy into law and mandating that all clinical research include women
and minorities and for data from phase III clinical trials to be analyzed by sex.
In 2014, the NIH issued a mandate that all funded preclinical studies had to represent males
and females, including animals, tissues, and cells. The policy considered sex a biologic variable
and required applicants to explain the manner in which sex is factored into research design
and analysis. The policy was introduced to recognize that the quality and generalizability of
research depends on the inclusion of important biologic variables, such as sex. At the same
time, preclinical research continued to rely heavily on male animals or exclude the variable of
sex.2
Has Progress Been Made?
Studies show that sex-specific analysis continues to fall short.
Enrollment of females in randomized controlled trials

Has Progress Been Made?
In assessing high-impact orthopaedic journals, the number of studies that include sex-
specific analysis has been increasing in the past two decades. However, the percentage
of studies overall remains low, with fewer than one-third of all studies including sex-
specific analysis.3 Stratification by sex may not be practical or feasible in all studies;
however, clinicians, educators, and researchers must promote and support data
stratification by sex in clinical and biomedical research, including non–NIH-funded
research. The publication of sex-specific analyses allows for hypotheses to be generated

regarding sex differences for future research and for systematic reviews to include this
subgroup information.
Recent literature shows that enrollment of females, elderly, and minorities in
randomized controlled trials remains low compared with their representation in the
general population based on census demographics.4,5 Failure to represent females in
these trials may result in limitations to the generalizability of study results.
Why Sex-Specific and Gender-Specific Analysis Matters
Sex matters in biomedical research because differences between males and females in
anatomy, physiology, presentation of pathology, and treatment outcomes have been found
throughout the field of orthopaedics.
The evidence is mounting for sex and gender differences in major causes of disease and
disability; however, persistent gaps in research remain.
Epidemiology
Although men are more likely to suffer traumatic injuries, women tend to be
disproportionately affected by disabling musculoskeletal conditions. These differences span all
phases of life: in infancy with developmental dysplasia of the hip, in adolescence with scoliosis
and anterior cruciate ligament rupture, and in adulthood with osteoarthritis and fragility
fractures. Disparities in the diagnosis and management of diseases also exist, with important
orthopaedic implications that affect women more commonly than men, such as Alzheimer’s
disease with increased fall risk leading to fragility fractures and lung cancer leading to bony
metastases.6 Additional clinical and biomedical research is necessary to explain the similarities
and differences in the incidence and presentation of these common orthopaedic conditions
between males and females and their response to treatment.
Risk of Harm
Biomedical research that fails to account for sex presents risk of harm because it is assumed
that the results apply to everyone.

This is demonstrated by one of the most infamous implant recalls in orthopaedics. In 2015,
Smith & Nephew removed the smaller sizes of the Birmingham Hip Resurfacing implant from
the market and contraindicated their use in women after performance data published in the
United Kingdom showed increased early failure rates in women compared with total hip
arthroplasty.7 Premarket studies failed to account for differences in sex and femoral head size,
which led to unsatisfactory outcomes and possible patient harm.
Women continue to be underrepresented in clinical trials, particularly in phase I and phase II
experimental drug trials, leading to a higher incidence of adverse effects in females and
limited pharmaceutical treatment options for pregnant women or women of reproductive
age.8
Tailored Treatment Options
Response to pain and treatment and the adverse effects of treatment also differ between
males and females. Failure to stratify by sex results in missed opportunities to discover these
differences and improve health by tailoring treatment options to males and females.
The research supporting many common treatment options for women, such as anti-
inflammatories, has been disproportionately performed on male participants.9 Molecular
mechanisms of inflammation differ among males and females.10 Additional understanding of
these biologic differences and responses to therapy based on differences in sex will improve
healthcare delivery.
Reproducibility
If the sex of cells, tissues, animals, and human subjects are not recorded or published in
literature, problems with reproducing the results may occur.
Defining the Terms
Sex
The NIH defines sex as the biologic differences between males and females, including
chromosomes, anatomy, and physiology.
Gender

The NIH defines gender as socially constructed roles and behaviors enacted within a cultural
and historical context. Individuals can identify as a gender different from their biologic sex or
sex assigned at birth.
Using These Terms in Scientific Research
In a research context, the terms sex and gender have been used interchangeably and
inconsistently in the past, which leads to confusion about research designs, outcomes, and
implications for practice.
In the 2016 American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons Annual Meeting, the term gender
was used 69% of the time to describe differences between males and females in
presentations, posters, and exhibits, whereas sex was used 31% of the time.11 This highlights
the need for additional education and exposure to these terms and their appropriate use in
research. Sex is the correct term to use in discussing the biologic difference between males
and females because it commonly is the goal in orthopaedic research. The term sex should be
used in examining the role that biologic factors play with regard to physiology, presentation,
treatment, and outcomes of orthopaedic conditions. Sex and gender interact with health in
various ways, and these variables can be categorized into sex- and gender-related variables.
Sex-related Variables
Sex-related variables are biologic factors affected by hormones and other cellular-driven
processes. These include height, weight, lean body mass, fat mass, muscle strength, peak bone
mineral density, hemoglobin, kidney function, etc. Some conditions are directly linked to the
sex chromosomes, such as Duchenne muscular dystrophy and hemophilia.
Gender-related Variables
Gender-related variables result from social/cultural influences.
These are the PROGRESS variables: place of residence, race/ethnicity/culture/language,
occupation, gender, religion, education, socioeconomic status, and social capital.
An example is the passage of Title IX of the Education Amendments Act of 1972. This
legislation states that “No person of the United States shall, on the basis of sex, be excluded
from participation in, be denied the benefits of, or be subjected to discrimination under any
education program or activity receiving Federal financial assistance.”12

As a result, female participation in collegiate sports and the incidence of sports-related injuries
in females have increased exponentially in the past four decades.
Designing Research Studies
Literature Review
In designing a research study, the first step is to review the literature. Determine if sex and
gender differences have been documented in epidemiology, risk factors, and/or outcomes.
Assess how researchers have measured and accounted for sex and gender differences in their
research design and analysis.
Any questionnaires should be valid in men and women.
Methods
Research design should use inclusion and exclusion criteria that consider sex/gender and
diverse populations of females and males.
Innovative recruitment strategies ensure adequate diversity and power in research studies.
Data collection should consider sex and/or gender as variables.
The sex of the animal model, tissue sample, or human subject should be identified clearly
and properly.
All relevant sex- and gender-related variables should be recorded.
Available gender scales include identity, roles, norms, and relations and can be used to
collect information in primary surveys and research. These scales/scores enable analysis of
gender independent from sex. If gender is not directly measured in the dataset, this variable
can be included by using sex-related associations, using second-level stratification by sex,
using gender-related variables, or creating a gender composite score to analyze gender
independent of sex.
Questionnaires should be validated in men and women, should not be gender biased, and
should be sensitive to gender issues.
Study design should account for the gender lens: the sex/gender of a research
assistant/interviewer may affect the dynamics and responses of interviews.
Analysis and Reporting

Studies should be designed with sufficient sample size to perform sex-specific analyses.
Analyses should be powered to detect sex differences.
Controlling for sex in multivariable regression is not that same as stratifying, or disaggregating,
by sex. Controlling for sex does not allow for exploration of data separately for men and
women. For differences in outcome between sexes, the multivariable regression adjusts for
sex, as if sex were held constant, resulting in an outcome that is an estimated average.
Stratified analyses should always be reported if a difference or an expected difference exists
between males and females.13
Drug efficacy, safety, and tolerability data should always be disaggregated by sex.
Translation
The study should evaluate the appropriate translation of results.
The terms sex and gender should be applied and reported appropriately. In general, in
biomedical research not involving human subjects, the term sex will be most appropriate.
The study should determine if conclusions and health interventions differ based on sex and/or
gender based on findings.
Summary
Musculoskeletal health is one of the areas in medicine in which the biologic differences
between males and females are most striking. To improve healthcare delivery, considerable
efforts are necessary to prioritize research that explores the influences of sex and gender on
orthopaedic conditions so that treatment can be tailored to the separate biologic and social
needs of our patients. Sex and gender are variables that must be considered in each phase of
a research study.
